633.dq: Asu & Teras 2009:370: "Primary stress in native Estonian words is fixed, falling almost always on the first syllable of a word" (word stress treated separately from the intonational pitch accents described under 'Rhythm and intonation', p.371).
633.dloc: Asu & Teras 2009: p.370, 'Prosodic features: Stress'; Asu & Lippus 2018: p.602 (Introduction); Hayes 1991:264 via StressTyp2 entry
633.heavy: Only the carried Hayes passage defines weight for stress: word-finally 'Heavy... is: CVV, CVVC, CVCC but not CVC' (ST1 note: 'heavy for rhythm: long vowels'); a ternary interval requires its second syllable to be light. The Tartu primary descriptions opened (Asu & Teras 2009; Asu & Lippus 2018) say only that secondary-stress placement depends on 'syllable structure' without defining heavy; Lippus et al. 2006 give trisyllabic [ˈpu.na.ˌseit] 'red ones' with secondary stress on a heavy (CVVC) final. Overlength (Q3) additionally licenses an immediately following secondary stress (Prillop 2013; ST1 remark).
633.dflt: Primary initial regardless of weight; in all-light words secondary stresses on odd-numbered syllables (3rd, 5th), with 3rd~4th-syllable variation in longer words and a final dactyl when the syllable count is odd (Lippus et al. 2006: 'the last stressed syllable is followed by two unstressed syllables').
633.prule: Primary stress fixed on the first syllable of the word in native vocabulary (quantity-insensitive); non-initial only in some loans/foreign words, interjections and names.
633.srule: Secondary stresses fall on successive odd-numbered syllables after the initial primary stress (3rd, 5th, 7th; syllabic trochees, feet of one to three syllables), with placement 'not always predictable': a secondary stress may directly follow the primary only in a Q3 (overlong) word (ohtlik, armsalt, aastaid); the final syllable of a word of three or more syllables takes secondary stress when it ends in a long plosive or a consonant cluster (raamatut, raamatust vs. raamatud); derivational suffixes (-mine, -line, -lik, -ik, -nna, -stik...) tend to attract secondary stress; otherwise 3rd~4th-syllable variation by morphology, speaker and phrase rhythm.

evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The survey treats Estonian's three quantity degrees as properties of the foot-initial stressed syllable, with overlength (Q3) a stress feature that goes with a sharp pitch and intensity fall, a shortened second-syllable vowel and, per Lehiste 1962 and Liiv 1961–62, a subglottal-pressure drop and tenser, more pharyngeally constricted articulation. It adds no new stress-position claim; the entry's fixed initial stress is consistent with every transcription and with 'the first syllable'.

evidence_works.work: Köhnlein & Ian S. Cameron 2024, What word-prosodic typology is missing: Motivating foot structure as an analytical tool for syllable-internal prosodic oppositions (Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 42(3): 1043-1079. doi:10.1007/s11049-023-09602-4)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: Theoretical comparison, no new data: the paper restates that Estonian Q2 vs Q3 (long vs overlong initial syllables) differs in duration and, in some intonational contexts, in where the H*L fall lands (late fall on Q2, early fall on Q3), and analyzes Q3 as a monosyllabic bimoraic foot and Q2 as a disyllabic foot with the initial syllable as head. This adds a quantity-conditioned pitch-alignment detail and foot analysis to the initial-stress entry and does not treat Estonian as having lexical tone, so the no-tone class stands.

evidence_works.work: Martínez-Paricio & Kager 2015, The binary-to-ternary rhythmic continuum in stress typology: layered feet and non-intervention constraints (Phonology 32(3): 459–504. doi:10.1017/S0952675715000287)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: Estonian is placed in the ternary-and-binary exhaustive class: dactyls from the left edge, one or two binary feet at the right edge so that every syllable is footed, initial stress primary. The entry's initial primary agrees; the entry gives secondary stress on the 3rd, 5th and 7th syllables with feet of one to three syllables, whereas this paper (relaying Hint 1973, no Estonian forms given) makes the ternary foot the preferred one.

tn.quote: The Estonian quantity system is a complicated prosodic phenomenon in which duration interacts closely with stress and pitch (Lehiste 1997). ... A crucial additional difference in distinguishing Q2 and Q3 lies in the realization of pitch in a metric foot, which in Q1 and Q2 is a step-down F0 contour ... while Q3 is associated with a fall early during the first syllable. ... The most common intonational pitch accent in Estonian is a high tone associated with a metrically strong syllable followed by a trailing low tone (H∗ +L).
tn.cite: Asu, Eva Liina & Pire Teras. 2009. Estonian. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 39(3): 367-372 (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S002510030999017X
tn.locator: pp. 370-371, 'Prosodic features': 'Quantity system' and 'Rhythm and intonation'
tn.note: No lexical tones posited: the Q2/Q3 F0 difference (step-down vs early fall in the stressed foot) is treated as a cue to the three-way quantity contrast; H*+L etc. are intonational pitch accents.

634.dq: Position of stress is predictable in terms of the phonotactic structure of the concrete word.
634.dloc: section 3.3.2.1 and 3.3.2.5, pp. 316-318; morphophonology of stress 3.5.1.2-3.5.1.3, p. 323
634.heavy: long vowels; and, word-medially only, a syllable closed by the first member of a consonant cluster/geminate ('a long vowel or a cluster of consonants in the middle of the stem' -> initial stress in disyllables; polysyllables: 'the syllable preceding this cluster'). Word-final closed syllables are never treated as heavy ('i:-ren, 'sa:-ren keep initial stress); 3.5.1.3 names only 'short vs long vowels of the stem' as the phonological conditioner; p.323: long-vowel stems 'as a rule' keep stress, short-vowel stems let it shift to case/tense suffixes. Closed-syllable weight is inconsistently applied in the author's own examples (tyg'de vs 'hal-ka; huk,ty-kte'chen, sil,ki-d'a'ran final).
634.dflt: final syllable (words of 3+ syllables with only short vowels; disyllables 'more often' second syllable)
634.prule: Stress 'not constant' but 'predictable in terms of the phonotactic structure of the concrete word': all-short-vowel words of 3+ syllables -> final syllable; disyllables with two short vowels -> mostly second syllable (some first: 'ulle, 'ollo, both with geminates); disyllable with a long vowel or medial cluster in the stem -> first syllable; disyllable with two long vowels -> second; polysyllable with short vowels and a consonant cluster -> the syllable preceding the cluster; certain suffixes (causative -vkAn, volitional -mu) always stressed.
634.srule: Some polysyllabic words have a secondary stress in addition to the final main stress: on the first syllable of a three-syllable word and on the second syllable of a four-syllable word (bo-ko'non 'he caught up with someone',ngi-na'kin 'dog', sil,ki-d'a'ran 'she washes up', huk,ty-kte'chen 'he was running'), i.e. two syllables before the main stress; optional ('Some... may'), no weight condition stated. Restated by Bulatova & Grenoble 1999: 5 as 'a secondary stress on the antepenultimate syllable' in polysyllables.

However, it is possible to state that stress in Evenki is not constant: its position in different words (and word forms) may vary from the first to the last syllable. morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and agglutinative: 'Evenki possesses a rich system of suffixal derivation. In fact, Evenki is the richest language of the Tungus-Manchu group as far as the number of suffixal morphemes is concerned' (Introduction, p.xxi); 'Verb morphology is predominantly a matter of suffixal derivation. As for verbal inflection, it is found in the system of fused tense/indicative mood markers and person/number markers occurring in pre-final and final positions respectively before any enclitics' (2.1.3, p.217); 'The order of nominal suffixes is the following: alienable possession + number + case + personal/reflexive possession' (2.1.1.1.1.5, p.145). No prefixes or proclitics appear…

634.cfw: Nedjalkov's 1997 reference grammar, the only full description available, states that Evenki stress is not fixed but predictable from the shape of the word (long vowels attract it, and in words of short vowels it falls toward the end) while admitting that the system needs more study; Morozova, Osipov and Androsova 2023 likewise treat a long first-syllable vowel as the stressed one, and the only different picture, Tsumagari 2009's initial stress with a weight-sensitive high pitch, describes Solon of Inner Mongolia, which its author regards as a separate language.

635.heavy: a long syllable = a long vowel or a diphthong ('simple or complex' long syllable); syllables are open (C)V/(C)V̄/(C)VV only, so codas play no role
635.dflt: penultimate syllable (of the measure; hence word-penult for the final measure)
635.prule: Accent falls on any long vowel or diphthong; in a measure without a long syllable it falls on the penultimate vowel; no measure ends in a short accented vowel; the only measure shapes are CV́CV, CVCV́CV, CV̄́, CVCV̄́. The final measure of a word/phrase thus has its accent on a final long syllable, else on the penult; the phrase peak ('primary accent' of the earlier word-based analyses) is 'usually the final measure' (ch.37 n.7) but not always: it moves for contrast (§40.2) and does not fall on a measure made up of a purely functional morpheme such as -taka (evaka.maCAla.taka: 'she explained it', §40.3; some speakers do accent the final measure instead, 'This problem needs further study', ch.40 n.3). Earlier statements Schütz reviews agree on placement: Hazlewood 1872 'invariably on the last syllable, or last but one'; Churchward 1941 'normal position... last syllable but one … A syllable containing a long vowel or a diphthong, however, is nearly always accented, no matter what its position may be'.
635.srule: Each non-peak measure of a longer form carries its own accent, placed like the primary: on a long vowel or diphthong if the measure has one, else on the measure-penult (measures are only CV́CV, CVCV́CV, CV̄́, CVCV̄́, so never more than two unaccented syllables in a row and no adjacent accents unless long). Schütz identifies traditional 'secondary accent' with 'the accented syllable on the preceding measure'; the division of a longer form into measures follows its morpheme make-up (particles join a following base, each root patterns as if it ended a basic phrase) and is not predictable from syllable count or word boundaries -- he rejects 'penultimate and alternate preceding vowels' as 'the Austronesian accent myth' -- and he regards the primary/secondary ranking as a phrase-level feature.
635.quote: [§41.1, p.613] The marking system used here is redundant; once the measure boundaries are marked in a text, the position of the accent can be determined: it occurs on any long vowel or diphthong; in measures without long syllables, it occurs on the penultimate vowel. ... Again, it must be emphasized that in terms of syllable count or “word” boundaries, accent is not predictable. Instead, it is accent that determines the boundaries of the measures. To state this important principle in another way: there are no rules to determine where accent falls, for the accents are present whenever anything…

evidence_works.detail: Fijian, after Hayes 1995, is the quantity-sensitive example of binary iteration: final if heavy else penult, every heavy syllable stressed, alternating light syllables leftwards with the count reset by each heavy. This agrees with the catalog's measure-based account from Schuetz 1985.

636.dq: Chapter title '9 Word-level Prosody'; 'Suomi, Toivanen & Ylitalo (2003) and Suomi & Ylitalo (2004) who carefully distinguished between stress and accent (i.e., stress was investigated in target words that were not accented)' and 'Primary stress is thus invariably associated with the initial syllable. But the largest prominence on a word occasionally falls on the last syllable, as in single-word u…
636.dloc: ch. 9.1 'Degrees of word stress and their phonetic realisation', p.75-77; syllable weight: ch. 7, Table 1, p.65
636.heavy: Heavy = polymoraic syllable, i.e. any syllable with a segment (V or C) after the nucleus vowel: CVC, CVV, CVVC, VC, VV, CVCC, VVC, VCC (Table 1, p.65); light = monomoraic (C)V. Both long vowels/diphthongs and coda consonants make a syllable heavy.
636.dflt: Primary: initial regardless of weight. Secondary (words of 4+ syllables): source says only 'Usually... on the third or the fourth syllable, and later in the word usually on every second syllable except the last one'; a final syllable can bear secondary stress only if heavy after a light syllable, so in an all-light word the final is never stressed. The all-light case is not stated separately (details deferred to Karlsson 1983:150-151; StressTyp2 notes an optional ternary interval in light sequences).
636.prule: Primary stress invariably fixed on the word-initial syllable (quantity-insensitive); apparent final prominence in single-word utterances KiiTOS!, NäkeMIIN!, AiVAN! treated as pragmatic accentuation, not exceptions (p.77).
636.srule: Words of four or more syllables only: secondary stress usually on the 3rd or 4th syllable, then usually on every second syllable except the last; a final heavy syllable may bear secondary stress if the preceding syllable is light. Placement depends on syllable weight and on morphological structure and is 'not fully predictable' (source defers to Karlsson 1983:150-151). Feet left-headed, e.g. »usko«matto«missa«kaan (three secondary stresses).
636.quote: [p.75] Three degrees of stress have been traditionally distinguished for Finnish: a syllable may be primarily stressed, secondarily stressed or unstressed. ... Primary stress is invariably fixed to the word-initial syllable of a word; apparent exceptions will be dispelled below. Secondary stresses occur in longer than trisyllabic words, and they are not fully predictable. Usually, secondary stress falls on the third or the fourth syllable, and later in the word usually on every second syllable except the last one; however, secondary stress may fall on a final heavy syllable if the preceding s…

evidence_works.work: Anttila 2017, Word stress in Finnish: Some new results (Handout, University of Utah Linguistics Colloquium, 16 Nov 2017: 12 pp.)
evidence_works.note: The stress rule on p.1 is given as a 'first approximation' after Carlson 1978 and Elenbaas & Kager 1999: initial primary stress, secondary stress on every other syllable, a light syllable skipped when the next syllable is heavy, skipping optional when that heavy syllable is final. The handout's own evidence is indirect: /t/-deletion in partitive plurals as a diagnostic of foot structure (pp.1-2, items 6-11), counted over 29,526 generated forms from Tuomi 1972 stems matched against Finnish web sites (7,632 forms with hits, about 9 million hits; p.2, item 14). It reports that the skipping clause 'leaks both ways' and that skipping shows intra-individual, gradient variation (p.1, items 4-5), and concludes 'Finnish word stress is almost entirely rhythmical' with sonority and prominence-clash tendencies (p.11, items 61-62). No instrumental measurement.

evidence_works.work: Anttila 2007, Word stress in Finnish (Handout, LSA Annual Meeting, Anaheim, 4-7 Jan 2007: 14 pp.)
evidence_works.note: States 'Primary stress is always initial. All the action is in secondary stress' (p.1, item 2), a binary pattern (every other syllable after primary stress) and a ternary special pattern (skip a light syllable before a heavy one, optionally when the heavy syllable is final) (p.1, items 3-4), analysed as binary trochaic feet from left to right with heavy syllables stressed (p.1, item 5); the literature listed is Carlson 1978, Elenbaas 1999, Elenbaas & Kager 1999, Hanson & Kiparsky 1996, Karttunen 2006, Karvonen 2005, Keyser & Kiparsky 1984, Kiparsky 2003, Sadeniemi 1949 (p.1, item 1). Notes 'Plenty of variation and apparent exceptions to the secondary stress rules' and 'Secondary stress is hard to hear or pin down by phonometric methods' (p.1, item 6). Own evidence: /t/-deletion between unstressed light syllables as a stress diagnostic, counted over all generated partitive plurals of about 23,000 vowel-final stems from Tuomi 1972 via Google hits, 9.3 million forms over 10,000 stems (p.2, items 10-12). Concludes that stress is sensitive to vowel sonority and prominence clash and that some long words may take a compound stress pattern (p.12, items 68-69). No instrumental measurement.

evidence_works.work: Arnhold & Aki-Juhani Kyröläinen 2017, Modelling the Interplay of Multiple Cues in Prosodic Focus Marking (Laboratory Phonology 8(1): 4, pp. 1–25. doi:10.5334/labphon.78)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The article's own measurements concern sentence-level focus marking, not word-stress placement: in 947 read SVO sentences by 17 speakers, narrow focus versus givenness was cued by F0 range (the strongest predictor), word duration, intensity range and the location of the F0 maximum, and the F0 peak of a focused word sat reliably on the first-syllable vowel while on given words it could fall anywhere in the word. Its word-stress statement (initial primary stress, weaker than in Germanic languages, duration the only confirmed cue) restates Iivonen 1998, Suomi et al. 2003, Ylitalo 2009 and Arnhold

evidence_works.work: Elenbaas & Kager 1999, Ternary rhythm and the lapse constraint (Phonology 16(3): 273-329. doi:10.1017/S0952675799003772)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The paper restates the standard description: primary stress fixed on the first syllable, secondary stress on every second syllable to the right except that a light syllable is skipped when the next one is heavy (closed or long-vowelled), and secondary stress on a final heavy syllable is optional; this matches the catalog's initial primary with weight-sensitive trochaic secondary. It is a theoretical OT analysis of previously published data with no instrumental measurement; the article is already listed under finn1318 in the bibliography.

ev.text: Fore has only one phonemic suprasegmental feature: pitch-accent, to which I shall refer simply as 'accent'. As in a stress system, the unit of accent placement is the syllable, even though the main diagnostic feature of Fore accent is pitch. An accented syllable incurs higher pitch, which may be either level or falling. ... Each morpheme has its own underlying accent patterning. The surface realisation of accent in words results from the combination of these underlying patterns. [p.20] There are two components to a morpheme's underlying accent. 637.dq: Unlike English, Fore's phenomenon changes the basic meanings of words (p.22); contrasted with 2.32: 'No contrastive intonation patterns occur ... Higher pitch associated with accent is the cause of departures from this [falling] pattern' (p.23).

637.heavy: none: the source states no syllable-weight criterion for accent placement; accent is an underlying lexical property of each morpheme (accented on one nucleus, unaccented, and/or inducing accent on a following syllable). Syllable length (long vowels, glides, prenasalised/glottal clusters) is mentioned only as determining rhythm/timing (2.32), not accent.

Accent is contrastive (minimal pairs by accent position and by accent vs no accent).

evidence_works.work: Yamada 2010, Speech community-based documentation, description, and revitalization: Kari'nja in Konomerume (PhD dissertation, University of Oregon: sec. 1.5.2 pp. 18-19; sec. 3.1.2 pp. 126-132)
evidence_works.detail: Community-based documentation of Kari'nja at Konomerume (Surinam), examples from recorded texts and elicitation (p. 125). The dissertation gives no stress rule of its own and does not dispute Hoff 1968: it states that 'the prosodic system in the language remains poorly understood' and that 'The phonetic realization of stress in Kari'nja is neither completely consistent nor completely predictable. What may be realized as glottalization in one environment may be vowel length in another. In addition, there appear to be ideolectal differences among speakers' (p. 131). It characterises the rhythmic layer, citing Gildea (in press): 'The prosodic system has been described as an iambic system... The foot structure, which differs from primary stress, is organized in such a way that the head of a foot gets prosodic prominence. However, the phonetic realization of prominence varies... A heavy first syllable does not effect the iambic system - the heavy syllable forms a foot on its own and subsequent syllables continue predictable patterns - but conditioning factors for a heavy first syllable is unpredictable' (pp. 131-132); a first-person possessor on a consonant-initial noun 'causes a morphophonemic stress shift to the first syllable' (p. 132); 'Hoff (1968) used stress to diagnose word boundaries' (p. 132). On p. 19 it lists 'the identification of primary and secondary stress' among areas needing investigation, quotes Gildea that in Cariban iambic systems the iambs predict secondary stress correlating with vowel length while primary stress rests on pitch excursion, says 'Hayes' model cannot account for the still more complex stress phenomena of Kari'nja, as described in Hoff (1968)', and promises an instrumental analysis of 2010 lab recordings 'to confirm and add acoustic detail to Hoff's (1968) transcriptions' - no measurements are reported.

evidence_works.work: van der Hulst & Visch 1992, Iambic lengthening in Carib (Linguistics in the Netherlands 9: 113-124)
evidence_works.detail: Metrical analysis of vowel-length distribution built entirely on Hoff 1968 ('All Carib data we present come from the comprehensive grammar by Hoff (1968)', p. 113; Hoff consulted personally, p. 113 n. 1). Accent placement is restated from Hoff: 'each word in Carib contains an accent (manifested as high pitch), which is located on the second heavy syllable in the word (where V:, VC and diphthong count as heavy). If there is only one heavy syllable, the accent is on the final syllable' (p. 113). Their own contribution is the foot structure behind the alternating vowel length: '(2) a Length is distinctive in the first syllable only; b The foot is a quantity sensitive iamb; c V:, VC and ViVj count as heavy; d The final syllable is extrametrical; e Degenerate (i.e. monomoraic) feet are not allowed; f Vowels in strong position are lengthened (but not in final syllables)' (p. 114), with at most two feet per word (p. 114), prefixes added after footing and suffixes before (pp. 118-120), and the possessive -rï treated as a circumfix (p. 120). They do not derive the accent: 'Although we did not present an analysis of accent placement (we just said that only two feet are assigned) a rule like "head of second foot or final syllable" gives the right result' (p. 123). They also record a residue in Hoff's dialect: 'In odd-numbered words CVC behaves initially as light with respect to iambic lengthening, but as heavy with respect to accent placement (sambú:ra not *sambu:ra...)', whereas 'in the (presumably innovative) dialect of other speakers of Carib (Hoff (p.c.) and Peasgood 1972) the expected pattern is realized' (p. 118). Foot heads are described as lengthened, not as bearing secondary stress, so sec_status is unaffected.

ev.text: Stress in Gayo is predictable and therefore non-phonemic. Stress is characterised by higher pitch and longer duration than unstressed syllables. Gayo has moraic iambic stress, i.e. primary word stress falls on the final syllable of the word; stress is shifting when suffixes are added. In this section, primary stress is indicated by a raised stress mark (ˈ) preceding the syllable. Secondary stress falls on the penultimate syllable, i.e. the syllable preceding the syllable bearing primary stress, and is indicated by a lowered stress mark (ˌ): anak [ˌaˈnãk] 'offspring' asu [ˌaˈsu:] 'dog' siut [ˌsɪˈʊt] 'burn' rëje [ˌrɤ:ˈdʒɤ:] 'king' iô [ˌɪˈjo:] 'afternoon' petukel [pəˌtʊˈkəl] 'pumpkin' i-pet-in…

contra.detail: Eades 2005 pp.30-31: petukel [pəˌtʊˈkəl] 'pumpkin'; p.30 prints sëbet /sabət/ [sə:ˈbət] 'companion'. Two primary descriptions are irreconcilable. (1) Eades 2005 (full modern fieldwork grammar): stress predictable, primary on the word-final syllable regardless of vowel quality (petukel, sëbet, bëden, sëdep all carry final primary stress on a schwa syllable; p.30 glosses the final syllable 'final…

640.dq: Phrase stress is slightly more pronounced than word stress. Phrase stress is placed on the last word of a phrase (Eades 2005:31); 'the word is the domain in which primary stress occurs on its final syllable' (Eades 2005:44).
640.dloc: Eades 2005 section 2.2.1.1 'Lexical stress' and 2.2.1.2 'Phrase stress', p.31; section 2.1.2.1.4, p.30; section 3.1 'Word', p.44. Hazeu 1907 p.xii via StressTyp2 entry (carried quote only).
640.heavy: Eades 2005: no weight criterion at all -- fixed final primary, penultimate secondary, including words whose final syllable has schwa after a full-vowel penult (petukel [pəˌtʊˈkəl] 'pumpkin', p.31) and after a lengthened schwa penult (sëbet [sə:ˈbət] 'companion', bëden, sëdep, p.30, where the final syllable is glossed 'final (i.e. stressed)'). Hazeu 1907:xii (StressTyp2 carried passage, hedged 'As a general rule one can assume'): penult stressed unless its vowel is schwa; i.e. heavy = full (non-schwa) vowel, light = schwa; ST1 note ': full vowels'.
640.dflt: Hazeu 1907: final syllable when penult (and antepenult) have schwa; Eades 2005: not applicable (always final)
640.prule: Eades 2005: primary word stress on the final syllable of the word, shifting rightward onto suffixes (labelled 'moraic iambic', no weight condition stated). Hazeu 1907 (carried): as a general rule the penultimate syllable unless its vowel is schwa; if both penult and antepenult have schwa, main stress on the final syllable.
640.srule: Eades 2005 (2.2.1.1, p.31): secondary stress on the penultimate syllable, i.e. the syllable immediately before the final primary; one secondary per word, also in longer words (anak [ˌaˈnãk], petukel [pəˌtʊˈkəl], i-pet-inum-en [ɪpətɪˌnʊˈmə̃n]). Eades & Hajek 2006 (p.113): the penult secondary 'indicates relative evenness of stress'; in longer words secondary stress can instead appear two syllables before the primary (muluahni [ˌmuluˈahni]). Hazeu 1907 (carried): when both penult and antepenult have schwa (main stress then final), the antepenult takes a weak secondary accent (sěděkah, sělěnsoeng).

640.cfw: Eades's 2005 reference grammar, restated in Eades & Hajek 2006, puts primary stress on the final syllable with secondary stress on the penult and reports that older speakers regard final stress as native, but Hazeu 1907 gives penultimate stress as the general rule (final only when the penult vowel is schwa), and Eades & Hajek 2006 themselves concede that the stress cues spread over the last two syllables so that the penult often sounds stressed in connected speech, leaving final stress the best-supported reading rather than a settled one.

641.dq: Godoberi contrasts with other languages discussed so far: it possesses word stress in addition to a tonal system. (Borise, sec. 2.3); StressTyp2-carried Kodzasov: 'Word stress is always placed on the syllable which bears this impulse'.
641.dloc: Borise preprint lingbuzz/004204, sec. 2.3, pp. 6-7 (citing Saidova 1973: 36, 39; Kibrik et al. 1996: 4, 6); corroboration: Kodzasov 2003 ICPhS p. 64 (open-text); StressTyp2-carried Kodzasov (forthc./1999) entry in this entry's source list
641.heavy: No quantity criterion stated for Godoberi. StressTyp's own field '' = 'stiffness of articulators (H tone); Art/Lex Accent, Breathy V' -- i.e. the conditioning features are stiff/slack (H/L) syllable register, an articulatory accent impulse (!), and breathy voice, not vowel length or coda. Kodzasov 2003 (p.64) lists 'syllabic weight' as one of three parameters for Avar noun stress and says Godoberi 'additionally' involves breathy voice, without defining heavy or stating a weight rule for Godoberi.
641.dflt: not applicable (no weight rule); for stems with only H/L properties Kodzasov gives initial stress in HH/LH strings, final in LL strings
641.prule: Nouns: several (Kodzasov 2003: nine) lexical accentual paradigms, some with fixed initial stress, others with stress mobile in declension; per Kodzasov (StressTyp2-carried): a syllable bearing the Articulatory Accent (!) is always stressed (few words have it); breathy-voice words take final stress; otherwise initial stress in HH and LH strings, final stress in LL strings; 'Lexical accents also seem to be necessary'. Borise: 'the rules of stress placement have not been established'; stress-based minimal pairs exist (basá/bása, ámi/amí). Verbs: final stress in all forms (H...H) except the aorist/simple past (HL, initial=penult in disyllables).
641.srule: Reported second-hand for verbs only: 'In four-syllable words a secondary rhythmical stress usually appears' (StressTyp2 Ghodoberi verbal entry, after Kodzasov 1999); which syllable carries it is not given. Not mentioned in Borise 2020 sec. 2.3 (pp. 6-7), Kodzasov 2003 (p. 64), Tatevosov 1999 (sec. 2.1.2) or van der Hulst et al. 2010 (pp. 480-481, 794-795); StressTyp2 codes the nominal entry 'secondary: Absent'.
641.quote: The stress and tone system in Godoberi is quite complex. Godoberi contrasts with other languages discussed so far: it possesses word stress in addition to a tonal system. For nominals, several accentual paradigms have been proposed, with fixed and mobile stress (Saidova 1973:36; Kibrik et al. 1996:4). ... the relevant suprasegmental feature has to do with the stiffness and slackness of articulators and/or spectral properties of vowels, and not pitch. Combinations of HH, LL and HL but not LH are attested ... Both H and L can carry stress, but the rules of stress placement have not been establi…

641.idn: Borise (primary source) treats 'Godoberi' as a single language with no dialect statement, summarizing Saidova 1973, Kibrik et al. 1996 and Tatevosov 1999. Tatevosov 1999 (held, read): the language of the villages Godoberi and Zibirkhali; the Zibirkhali sub-dialect shows some mainly phonetic differences from the…
641.exq_: For nominals, several accentual paradigms have been proposed, with fixed and mobile stress ... Both H and L can carry stress, but the rules of stress placement have not been established. ... Verbal accentual system in Godoberi is much simpler: ... most verb forms consist of H syllables and have fin…
641.tone: Quasi-tonal register coexisting with word stress: Kibrik et al. 1996 specify every syllable as H or L (HH, LL, HL attested, not LH), but they and Tatevosov 1999 describe the feature as stiffness/slackness of articulators, not pitch; Saidova 1973 treats Godoberi as stress-only; Borise: the labels 'high'/'low' are pre-theoretical. Stress placement in nouns is partly conditioned by this register (StressTyp2-carried Kodzasov: initial stress in HH/LH strings, final in LL).

Word stress is always placed on the syllable which bears this impulse [Articulatory Accent] ... Breathy voice motivates final stress. ... the initial syllable receives stress in HH and LH strings and the final syllable in LL strings.' Verbs: 'Disyllabic roots have a standard prosodic pattern HH which does not change in declensional forms with the sole exception of the aorist, where a HL-pattern is found. Stress placement corresponds to the tonal structure: only the aorist has initial stress, all…
morph.elicq: No accessible statement of how stress was elicited: Kodzasov's 'Phonological preliminaries: 4. Word prosody' (Kibrik ed. 1996: 4-6, from the 1993 MSU field trip) is not open. The evidence cited in the accessible sources is isolated word forms and minimal pairs ('There are stress-based minimal pairs: basá "say/sing.IMP", bása "say.PST.3SG.M": ámi "wooden dish", amí "eat.INF" (Saidova 1973: 39)', Borise 2018:6), and Borise 2018 notes for the Dagestanian tonal/stress accounts generally that 'the tonal accounts have been difficult to assess, due to scarcity of instrumental evidence. Such evidence is still largely missing'.
morph.stmt: Godoberi is 'an agglutinative language (with rich nominal and verbal morphology), but with some elements of fusion (in word formation) and analytics (in structure of some separate verb forms)' (minlang.iling-ran.ru, after Saidova); all nominal inflection (oblique stem, plural, grammatical and bimorphemic spatial cases) and all verbal TAM, negation, non-finite and derivational (causative -ali, verbalizer -ɬi, masdar -ir) marking is suffixal, the only prefixes being the single-consonant gender/number agreement markers w-/j-/b-/r- found on a minority (c. 24%) of verbs and a few adjectives/adverbs -- StressTyp's Kodzasov entry: 'I have not encountered any prefixes.'

642.dq: Each word carries only one primary stress, the placement of which is determined by the tone pattern of the word ... (p.5); contrasted with the phrase: 'A phonological phrase in Golin consists of one or more phonological words with an optional nuclear syllable marked by stress ... However on any word it occurs only on the normally stressed syllable of the word' (pp.5-6).
642.heavy: Not syllable quantity: the stress-attracting property is lexical HIGH TONE ('Stress occurs on the final high tone of a word, and in the absence of a high, it occurs on the final low'). Closed syllables (only l, m, n close syllables) and the close-knit glide nuclei ay/aw (one syllable, one tone) are not said to attract stress; two-vowel sequences such as /ai/, /au/ carry two tones and count as two syllables (sec. 2.1-2.2, p.4). None of this conditions stress placement.
642.prule: One primary stress per phonological word, placed on the final (rightmost) high-toned syllable of the word; if the word has no high tone, on the final syllable.
642.srule: None: 'Each word carries only one primary stress' (Bunn & Bunn 1970, sec. 3, p.5); syllables are only stressed or unstressed and no secondary or rhythmic stress is mentioned (secs. 2-4 and notes read).
642.quote: [2.3.1, pp.4-5] High tone has three allotones, conditioned by its occurrence with stress, or its occurrence on unstressed syllables. Stress occurs on the final high tone of a word, and in the absence of a high, it occurs on the final low. ... [3. WORD, p.5] The phonological word is composed of one or more syllables. Each word carries only one primary stress, the placement of which is determined by the tone pattern of the word as described in section 2.3.1. Thus stress occurs on the final syllable of ... onibá 'snake', ..., on the medial syllable of síbági 'sweet potato type', gomági 'type of …
642.loc: sec. 2.3.1, p. 4; sec. 3 'Word', p. 5; sec. 4 'Phrase', pp. 5-6; footnote 7, p. 7 of Pacific Linguistics A-23 (sealang online edition)
642.idn: Golin, 'a sub-dialect of the Marigl dialect of the Dom language' (the source distinguishes four Marigl sub-dialects: Golin, Kia (Sa), Keri, Gunaa); data from Kone village (a named variety of the language); data: village of Kone, four miles east of the Gumine Sub-District Office, Chimbu District, T.N.G.; material…
642.exq_: There is contrastive stress on words with the tone pattern ´´ˋ. Those words not following the general pattern are all compounds in which the stress occurs on the first high tone of the word: pú 'blow' mugu 'container' --> 'púmúgu 'flute'. This is in contrast with ´´ˋ tone pattern tárámbi 'taro type…
642.tone: Two tonemes, high and low, one per syllable: 'Each syllable has one toneme, high or low: kúbá 'stick', kuba 'vegetable type', golín 'old', gólín 'finished off edge of bag'' (sec. 2.3, p.4; high tone written with an acute, low unmarked, fn. 3); word-stress placement is itself determined by the tone pattern (final high-toned syllable, else final syllable; sec. 2.3.1). High tone has three allotones and low tone three, conditioned by stress (sec. 2.3.1-2.3.2, pp.4-5). Tone sandhi 'does occur within words, conditioned by suffixation of one class of noun stems and verb stems, and within phrases when descriptives precede nouns' but is not described (sec. 2.3.3, p.5).

643.dq: It will be convenient to define the phonological word as a sequence of syllables / morae over which the above rules of stress assignment apply. (McGregor 1990:123); p.119 separates stress from pitch: 'a syllable may be loud or may have high pitch without being stressed. For instance, the final ... high pitch may occur on -mi END (when final in a tone unit)'.
643.dloc: McGregor 1990 pp.119-123 (sec. 2.5, 2.5.1; mora rules S1/S2 on pp.122-123); Kager 1992 pp.127-129
643.heavy: Bimoraic syllables: closed syllables CVC and open syllables with a long vowel (CVV) count two morae; open CV with short vowel counts one (McGregor 1990:122). p.123: stressed non-initial syllables are those that are 'closed' or where the syllable 'has a long vowel or is closed'. Kager 1992:127 carries: 'bimoraic root minimum (where closed syllables count as heavy)'.
643.dflt: initial (SU, SUU; plus penult in 4-5 syllable words: SUSU, SUUSU)
643.prule: Stress is non-distinctive and 'always predictable'. Default is initial stress (bisyllables SU; trisyllables mostly SUU 'the most frequent pattern'; 4 syllables 'the norm is for the first and third syllables to be stressed'; 5 syllables SUUSU). McGregor's analysis (pp.122-123): count morae (CV=1, CVV/CVC=2), map SU / SUU / SUSU / SUUSU (SUUSUU, SUUSUSU, SUUSUUSU per Kager's carry) onto the mora string; S1 a syllable is stressable if one of its morae is stressed; S2 of two successive stressable syllables only one is stressed, 'usually the one with the most morae'. Net effect: in trisyllables a heavy (long/closed) second syllable after a light first takes the stress (USU: bil'gaali, ma'ndaadda, ga'rajbi), and heavy (closed) final syllables in 3-4 syllable words are stressed (SUS, SUUS). Which of two stresses is primary is variable: in SUS 'the final syllable usually bears primary stress, although it is sometimes the initial syllable'.
643.srule: Two stresses per word where the mora template gives two S positions (SUS, SUSU = 1st+3rd, SUUSU = 1st+4th); the non-primary one is usually the INITIAL stress, since the final of SUS and the third syllable of SUSU 'usually' bear primary stress, but the ranking may reverse or level ('kurra'ngkul ~,kurra'ngkul ~ 'kurra,ngkul;papu'rrungku ~ 'papu'rrungku); five-syllable roots are written with two primary marks ('lawaki'mana); beyond five morae 'not clear' (SUUSUU suggested).

[p.120] (ii) In addition to an initial stress, a trisyllabic word may have a stressed final syllable (SUS). In this case, the [p.121] final syllable usually bears primary stress, although it is sometimes the initial syllable that is the strongest stressed ... (iii) ... trisyllabic word bears stress, while the first syllable is unstressed (USU). Some examples are: bil'gaali ma'ndaadda ga'rajbi ... [p.122] A syllable…
643.loc: McGregor 1990 pp.119-123 (sec. 2.5, 2.5.1; mora rules S1/S2 on pp.122-123); Kager 1992 pp.127-129
643.idn: Gooniyandi (spelt Kuniyanti in the 1984 thesis), Bunaban, spoken by about 100 people mainly in the Fitzroy Crossing area, southern Kimberley, Western Australia (Gogo-Bayulu, Yiyili, Junjuwa); McGregor finds 'too few differences to identify dialects' (1984 sec. 1.3 p.5); data: McGregor 1984 sec. 1.10 p.18: 'This study…
643.exq_: Beyond five morae it is not clear exactly how stress is assigned, there being too few examples. ... S2 If two successive syllables are stressable, only one of them may receive stress, and it is usually the one with the most morae.

Section 2.5.1 is titled 'Stress in simple roots' ('Simple (unreduplicated) roots ... have at least one stressed syllable', p.120). On complex words, p.125: 'stress is assigned first to the root as an independent word, and then to the root plus morpheme as a single unit. In case this gives rise to a sequence of stressed syllables, the second syllable in the sequence loses its stress (cf. S2) ... When added to a word of four syllables the stress pattern of the root is unchanged. For example, 'warli'biddi-ya 'river-LOC''; p.125-126: 'a stressed syllable in a bound morpheme is frequently…
morph.elicq: Isolated elicited words plus auditory observation of speech, explicitly non-instrumental: p.120 '[final] syllables of isolated, elicited words often have higher pitch than the preceding syllables, for example, the following pronunciations were elicited: doomboo ['tombu] 'owl', doomoodoo ['tomotu] 'chest''; p.119 'Stressed syllables tend to sound louder, and to have higher pitch than unstressed syllables; they are probably also uttered with greater pulmonic air pressure (there is however no instrumental evidence to back up this suggestion)'; p.128 'Sequences of up to three consecutive stressed syllables have been heard: 'ward'ba'ngadda (go-FUT+A-(1sg)O) 'you'll bring it to me' and…
morph.stmt: All bound marking follows the lexical root: NPs take phrase-final enclitic postpositions for case and number ('Postpositions... enter into syntagmatic relations with phrases... to form units of phrase rank', McGregor 1990 p.276; 14 enclitic postpositions, p.174), and the finite verb is lexical verb root (+ aspect/mood suffixes) + a 'classifier complex' in which pronominal and tense PREFIXES attach to a bound classifier root, the whole forming one phonological word after the verb root (pp.191, 203-221) — hence Capell's label, quoted p.1, of Gooniyandi and Bunuba as 'prefixing languages without noun classification' refers to prefixes on the post-verbal classifier, not on the lexical root…

This is especially manifest when nouns are used in their vocative forms, which targets the penultimate syllable for high tone, followed by low tone on the final syllable. ... The noun in Gorwaa is therefore a metrical domain. (p. 222) ... Phonologically, the noun is reliably a metrical domain for syllabi…

(2.15)-(2.16); p. 100 and p. 162 (tonic pronouns 'have stress and tone'); p. 137 (selectors 'bear no stress'); ch. 4, secs. 4.3.3 and 4.3.5, pp. 222 and 224 (the word/noun as the metrical domain for syllabification and stress assignment)
644.heavy: A long vowel in the penult ('If the penult contains a long vowel, then it is stressed instead'); p. 82 restates it as a long vowel (or high tone) in the second syllable. Closed syllables are not mentioned as stress-attracting; a final long vowel does NOT attract stress in the p. 79 rule (lawalaa 'spear' has first-syllable stress). Separately, a high-toned final syllable attracts stress when the penult vowel is short (tone-conditioning, not weight). Epenthetic vowels never bear stress.

Epenthetic second-syllable vowels never take stress; a second syllable with a long vowel or high tone is stressed (p. 82, after Mous 1993:27 on Iraqw).

644.idn: Gorwaa (ISO 639-3 gow; = Gorowa, Goroa, Fiome/Ufiomi in older literature); data: Babati district (Manyara Region), north-central Tanzania; author's fieldwork from 2012 to the time of writing (2018), based mainly in and around Endabeg village; 126 participants recorded (oldest b. 1912, youngest b. 2003)
644.tone: Gorwaa has lexical and grammatical pitch accent (level pitch accent = low on all syllables; rising pitch accent = high tone on the final syllable of the phonological word; nouns possess LPA or RPA lexically, plus three intonational contours), described separately from stress; the stress rule refers to tone (a high-toned final syllable is stressed when the penult vowel is short), and tonic pronouns 'have stress and tone' while selectors 'bear no stress and are assigned no tone'.

Also §2.2.5.3 (p.82): "The vowel of the initial syllable receives stress if the vowel of the second syllable is epenthetic ... morph.stmt: Gorwaa lexical words are suffixing: "nouns are formed of at least three identifiable subparts: the stem (STM), the suffix (SFX), and the linker (L)" (§4.2, p.213), with possessive/demonstrative/indefinite determiners, topic =oo and negative =ká(ng) following as suffixes/enclitics, and all verbal derivation (causative -iis, durative -iim, middle -iit, factitive -uus/-ees, inchoative -uw) and person/number/mood/negation inflection realised as stem-final endings, suffixes and pitch accent; the only pre-root material is the stressless, toneless preverbal 'selector' — "a null auxiliary verb surrounded by a series of clitics" in which "Gorwaa indexes all core arguments as proclitics to the…

tones: level pitch accent (LPA): low tone on all syllables
rising pitch accent (RPA): high tone on the final syllable of the phonological word
tn.quote: Kießling (2004), establishes that across South Cushitic there are two predominant phonemic tone contours, which operate within phonological words including the subject noun, as well as the vP. … The two ‘grammatical’ contours described by Kießling (2004), and which bear the largest functional loads by far, are level pitch accent (LPA), in which default low tone is assigned to all syllables of a domain, and rising pitch accent (RPA), in which prominent high tone is manifested on the final syllable of the phonological word. Nouns may possess LPA or RPA lexically.
tn.cite: Harvey, Andrew David. 2018. The Gorwaa Noun: Toward a description of the Gorwaa language. PhD thesis, SOAS University of London (author's copy, andrewdtharvey.com).
tn.locator: ch. 2 'A grammatical sketch of Gorwaa', sec. 2.2.3 'Pitch and intonation', pp. 76-77; exx. (2.4)-(2.5) pp. 77-78; stress sec. 2.2.4 p. 79
tn.note: Two lexical word melodies the author calls pitch accents: level (all syllables low) vs rising (high on the word-final syllable); stress is separate, drawn to a final high or a long penult.

644.cfw: Harvey's 2018 SOAS dissertation, the only modern first-hand description of Gorwaa, states the rule with examples (stress on the first syllable by default, on the penult when its vowel is long, on the final syllable when the penult is short and the final carries high tone), and Harvey and Mreta 2016, the same author writing on Swahili loanwords, fits that rule (a lengthened penult takes the stress) while no other source describes Gorwaa stress at all.

645.dq: 1.5.2. Word-Stress: Stress in Gujarati has been little explored and in what follows a minimal overview of stress will be provided. (word stress treated separately from 1.5.3 Intonation, which gives four phrase-level pitch contours)
645.heavy: Vowel quality plus closure: /a/ attracts stress most strongly; other full vowels (e, ɛ, i, o, ɔ, u) beat 'weak' /ə/; a syllable with /ə/ is stress-repelling when open but takes stress when closed ('if the /ə/... is a closed syllable, it takes the stress'; trisyllables: second-syllable /ə/ throws stress to the first 'However if the second syllable is closed, it is the second, which takes the stress'). /i/ in the second syllable of trisyllables behaves 'nearly similar' to /ə/. No vowel-length criterion.
645.dflt: disyllables with identical vowels (incl. both /ə/): first syllable; trisyllables: penult (second syllable) 'as a general rule'; 4+ syllables: normally second syllable
645.prule: Monosyllables: on the vowel. Disyllables: same vowel in both -> first; V2 not /a/ -> first, unless V1 is open-syllable /ə/ (then second); closed-syllable /ə/ in first -> first; V2 = /a/ -> second; both /a/ -> first favoured; both /ə/ -> first ('some speakers... interchangeably'); second syllable a grammatical marker -> first. Trisyllables: final never stressed; general rule penult (second); first if it has /a/; first if second has /ə/ (or /i/, unless first has /ə/), unless the second is closed (then second); both first two /ə/ -> first; both /i/ -> free. Four+ syllables (rare): normally the second syllable.
645.srule: Not mentioned in Doctor 2004, section 1.5.2 'Word-Stress', pp.15-16 (one stress position per word given for 1-, 2-, 3- and 4+-syllable words; no secondary or rhythmic stress discussed). Later instrumental studies (Shih 2018; Bowers 2019) do not discuss secondary stress either.

645.cfw: Doctor 2004 and Cardona 1965 describe a vowel-quality-sensitive system in which /a/ attracts stress and open-syllable schwa repels it, but the two independent acoustic studies, Shih 2018 and Bowers 2019, find only weakly cued fixed initial stress (penultimate in disyllables) with no sensitivity to vowel quality, and Shih and de Lacy 2019 show that the thirteen impressionistic descriptions contradict one another on almost every point, so the type of system is still an open debate in which the acoustic evidence leans toward fixed initial stress.

646.heavy: Holes 2010: 'long' syllables = CVV, CCVV, CVVC, CVVCC, CVCC (long vowel anywhere, or word-final vowel + CC / long vowel + C); 'short' = CV, CCV, CVC; when no long syllable is present a 'closed' (CVC) penult takes stress in trisyllables (warágtik, sharábna) while all-open words stress the antepenult (báraka); a CVV syllable outranks a following closed CVC (sháafatkum by rule, shaafátkum as variant). Feghali 2008: the last sequence 'of a short vowel plus two consonants or a long vowel plus a consonant, //VCC// or //VVC//' (non-final CVC.C counts, word-final CVC does not, final CVCC/CVVC does). Qafisheh 1977 (carried): final syllable 'long' (ST1 note: = long vowels).
646.dflt: Holes 2010: penult in disyllables (smícha, sábab) and antepenult in words of three or more open syllables (báraka), with stated variation mádrasa ~ madrása for CVC-CV-CV; Feghali 2008: first syllable (identical outputs for the 2-3-syllable words cited); Qafisheh 1977 as carried: penult. No source cites an all-light word longer than three syllables (syncope).
646.prule: Holes 2010: stress the only long syllable (CVV or CVVC, CCVV; word-final CVCC, CVVC or CVVCC); if two long syllables, the last; if none, the penult in disyllables and in trisyllables with a closed (CVC) penult, the antepenult in words of three or more open syllables. Feghali 2008: stress the last //VCC// or //VVC// sequence, else the first syllable (same outputs for the 2-3-syllable words exemplified). Qafisheh 1977 as carried by StressTyp2: final syllable if long, otherwise penult.
646.srule: Not mentioned in Holes 2010 ('Syllable types and stress' and 'Stress exercise', pp. xxiv-xxvi; App. 1(E) pp. 378-379): one stressed syllable is marked per word, also in words of four to six syllables (kuwaytiyyíin, tistahlikíin, isti9laamáat, mu9taqadáatah); no secondary or rhythmic stress is described.

morph.elicq: p.xxiv: 'The stressed syllable in individual words of more than one syllable is marked superscript (e.g. á) throughout the text. The placement rules (sec. 1.2, p. 9; the section heading is on p. 8 and the example discussion runs on to p. 10) are stated as rules without a described procedure: 'Stress falls on the ultimate syllable if it is long' (long vowel, consonant cluster or geminate; /Xal'li:/, /sa:'fart/, /si'katt/); 'If the penult and the antepenult are short... open syllables of the form CVCVCV(C), stress falls on the antepenult' (/'madalan/); 'Otherwise stress falls on the penult' (/'sikat/, /mad'risi/); 'Stress has no phonological, morphological or syntactical function in Arabic' (p. 9). The instrumental part (sec. 6.5) measured the duration of vowels in stressed vs unstressed syllables in polysyllabic words from a one-word list and a phrase list, two subjects (FB, HJ), and found (p. 433) that 'stress has a significant effect on the duration of the long vowels /i:/ and /a:/ and that it has no or little effect on the duration of the short vowels /i/ and /a/' (e.g. FB, isolated words, prose p. 433 and Table 6.5.1 p. 434: /i:/ 130.90 msec unstressed vs 156 msec stressed; /i/ 60.14 vs 65.11 msec, non-significant); summary point 7, p. 464: 'Stress has a significant effect on the duration of long vowels only... while it has no effect on the duration of short vowels'. The measurement takes stress position from the sec. 1.2 rules; it does not test placement.

647.dq: The stress is expiratory and strong. It is predictable; consequently, nonphonemic. Words containing no geminate vowel phonemes or diphthongs have the stress on the initial syllable. (Poppe 1970: 47; compound stress 2.13 and clause pitch/emphatic accent 2.15 are treated separately.)
647.heavy: geminate (long) vowel phoneme or diphthong (Poppe); Walker: 'heavy syllable (a syllable with a long vowel or diphthong)'. Closed syllables with short vowels are not heavy.
647.prule: Poppe 1970: no long vowel/diphthong -> initial syllable; exactly one long vowel/diphthong -> stress on it (including word-final, e.g. galuu, dalae); more than one -> stress on the penultimate long vowel/diphthong. Walker 1997 (own recordings + Bosson p.c.) sharpens 'penultimate' to: rightmost nonfinal heavy; final syllable only if it is the sole heavy; else initial.
647.srule: Walker 1997 (one Ulaanbaatar speaker, 1994, + Bosson p.c.): every heavy syllable (long vowel or diphthong) not bearing the primary stress carries a secondary stress, a word-final heavy included (u:rtaega:r H-sec H-prim H-sec); the initial syllable possibly also carries a secondary stress when not primary, posited only tentatively (durational/articulatory initial emphasis, pitch variable). Weight-placed, not rhythmic. Not mentioned in Poppe 1970, sec. 2.13-2.15 (pp. 46-47).

ev.text: As in Levantine Arabic the major word stress in BHA is located on one of the last three syllables of the word--essentially the rightmost heavy syllable, otherwise the third last. Heavy syllables are those containing a long vowel (CVV) or a short vowel plus consonant (CVC), while light syllables contain a single short vowel CCV). At the stage of the derivation where stress is assigned extraheavy CWC and CVCC are only found in final position, where they naturally also take the major stress. A final CVC syllable counts as light in BHA, as ^n many other languages. 648.dq: As in Levantine Arabic the major word stress in BHA is located on one of the last three syllables of the word--essentially the rightmost heavy syllable, otherwise the third last.
648.dloc: pp. 128-130 (section on accent, exx. (46)-(51)); secondary-stress footnote 5, p. 145
648.heavy: Heavy = long vowel (CVV) or short vowel + coda consonant (CVC); light = CV. Word-final consonant ignored for weight, so final CVC counts as light while final CVVC and CVCC ('extraheavy') count as heavy and take main stress.
648.dflt: antepenult ('otherwise the third last'); foot analysis (L->R trochees, rightmost foot head) yields penult in H-L-L-L words
648.prule: Main word stress on one of the last three syllables: the rightmost heavy syllable (final only if CVVC/CVCC, since final CVC is light by final-consonant extrametricality), otherwise the antepenult; in heavy-light-light-light words (3sg.f. perfect + V-initial object suffix, e.g. 9allamatuh) stress is penult, derived by binary left-dominant (trochaic) feet built left-to-right with the final foot carrying main stress. Stress is assigned before elision, so some surface forms are opaque (shabatak < sahabatak with main stress on -at- and secondary on the initial).
648.srule: Secondary stress reported but not reliably placed: the authors state that 'reliable judgements on secondary stresses are difficult to make'; the one clear case is an initial secondary accent in shàbátak-type forms (< sahabatak, head of an elided pre-tonic foot), and an initial secondary is transcribed in H-L-L-L words (9àllamátuh, bàarakátuh); in their analysis heads of left-to-right binary trochaic feet before the main-stress foot are 'reduced to secondary or suppressed'; pre-tonic prominence in dual nouns (maktabéen, fallaahéen) could not be separated from syllable weight.
648.quote: As in Levantine Arabic the major word stress in BHA is located on one of the last three syllables of the word--essentially the rightmost heavy syllable, otherwise the third last. Heavy syllables are those containing a long vowel (CVV) or a short vowel plus consonant (CVC), while light syllables contain a single short vowel CCV). At the stage of the derivation where stress is assigned extraheavy CWC and CVCC are only found in final position, where they naturally also take the major stress. A final CVC syllable counts as light in BHA, as ^n many other languages. If final consonants are ignored …

648.idn: The cited work (Irshied & Kenstowicz 1984) describes Bani-Hassan Arabic, a Bedouin dialect of c.130,000 speakers in northern Jordan (Zarqa-Mafraq-Jarash), not Hassaniyya (Glottolog hass1238, ISO mey, Mauritania/W. Sahara); the key was inherited from WALS 'ahs' = 'Arabic (Bani-Hassan)', which WALS itself maps to ISO…
648.exq_: Stress is on the third mora from the end of the word, e.g., on the first syllable in mäktäb ‘desk’, on the second in mäktūb ‘written’. It is strongly marked only on long vowels (accent of length rather than intensity). A lot of grammatical morphemes are clitics.

morph.stmt: p.109: 'BHA distinguishes perfect from imperfect; subject agreement is marked by suffixes in the perfect and a combination of suffixes and prefixes in the imperfect, the prefixes inducing certain alterations of the basic root shape. There is also a series of clitic suffixes marking nominal complements on verbs as well as nouns.' — i.e. mixed: inflection predominantly suffixal/enclitic (subject in the perfect, object, possessor, feminine, dual/sound plural), prefixal imperfect person markers, definite article and derived-measure markers (in-, ta-, i-, sta-), with extensive non-concatenative (templatic/ablaut, broken plural, gemination) morphology.

649.heavy: syllables containing a long vowel or a diphthong (or both) are heavy; syllables with a single short vowel are light (Hawaiian has no codas)
649.prule: All heavy syllables (long vowel or diphthong) are stressed, stress falling on the first vowel of the heavy syllable; otherwise stress is 'typically perceived on a penultimate short vowel' (liona [liˈona] vs loina [ˈloina]; final-heavy words stressed finally). Rightmost stress = penult, or final if the final syllable is heavy.
649.srule: Every heavy syllable (long vowel or diphthong) is stressed wherever it stands, so non-final heavies carry secondary stress ([ˌhaːˌpɐimeˈmeue] 'to praise'). Light syllables before the main stress are stressed 'depending on metrical position' but not by regular right-to-left trochees: five-syllable all-light words split about evenly between /ma.ˈku.a.ˈhi.ne/ (2nd + 4th) and /ˈʔe.le.ma.ˈku.le/ (1st + 4th) (Parker Jones 2018:107, 111). Schütz 2010:406-409 and Kettig 2021:66-67 state the same facts as: secondary stress on the accented syllable of every non-final measure (heavy syllable, or penult of a light-syllable measure), measures.

Pitch accents are represented through the use of a single H (high) or L (low) tone or a combination of the two. The stressed tone has an addition of an asterisk, i.e., H* or L*. … Note that the question and the statement have identical structure, it is the intonation that differentiates the statement from the question.

(Al Solami 2022 sec.4); 'The tendency to assign word stress to the right-most ...' / 'Due to the lack of secondary stresses in Hijazi' (Al-Mohanna 2004).

650.heavy: Heavy = CV: (long vowel) or closed CVC in non-final position ('CVC syllable is heavy except in final position where it is considered a light syllable'); superheavy = CV:C and CVCC, which attract stress word-finally; final CV and CVC never stressed (extrametrical).
650.dflt: Urban Hijazi: penult or antepenult, whichever is an even number of syllables from the word start/preceding heavy (ká.ta.bu antepenult, ba.ga.rá.ti penult, sá.ma initial); Bani Sulaim Bedouin: penult in trisyllables (ʔa.ká.lat), initial in light disyllables (kí.tab).
650.prule: Stress a final superheavy (CV:C, CVCC); otherwise a heavy (CV:, CVC) penult; otherwise a heavy antepenult; otherwise (all relevant syllables light) Urban Hijazi stresses penult or antepenult by even-syllable count from the preceding heavy/word start (sá.ma, ká.ta.bu, ba.ga.rá.ti; moraic trochees, End Rule Right, never beyond antepenult), while Bedouin Bani Sulaim stresses the penult in LLL (ʔa.ká.lat) and the initial in light disyllables (kí.tab; iambs with final-syllable extrametricality). Monosyllables are superheavy and stressed.
650.srule: None: 'Due to the lack of secondary stresses in Hijazi' (Al-Mohanna 2004: 18 fn.11, Urban Hijazi). Not mentioned in Al Solami 2022 (Bani Sulaim Bedouin; sec.3-4 and Appendix A read: one stress marked per word, e.g. [sa:.ʕad.tú:.hin], no statement on secondary stress).

651.dq: Hirdu has accent entirely as a part of intonation. A word may not have accent in a many-word contour-span. A word has always an accent in a single-word contour-span. The syllable which bears the accent on a word may be called the tonic. Even when the word bears no accent the tonic is slightly more prominent than the other syllables. (Kelkar 1968: 26)
651.heavy: Three ascending grades: Light = syllable ending in a short vowel (ɪ ʊ ə); Medium = syllable ending in a long vowel (i e u o a) or short vowel checked by a single nonsyllabic; Heavy = any other syllable (long vowel + coda, short vowel + two codas). Nasalization ignored.
651.dflt: penult (all syllables equal => all are maxima => last but one, e.g. sə"mɪ.tɪ 'committee' L"LL, ro"za.na M"MM)
651.prule: Tonic = the maximally heavy syllable of the word on the scale Light < Medium < Heavy; if several syllables tie for maximum, the last but one of the maxima is tonic (so a unique final maximum takes the tonic, e.g. kɪ"dʰər L"M, 'ɪn.qɪ"lab 'ML"H; ties go to the penultimate maximum, e.g. "roz.gar "HH, ro"za.na M"MM, sə"mɪ.tɪ L"LL).
651.srule: Subtonic (secondary, marked ') per Kelkar: with a unique weight maximum as tonic, the other syllables before and after it are alternately atonic and subtonic counting outward from the tonic, those adjacent to the tonic being atonic ('ɪn.qɪ"lab 'ML"H, "šox.ǰə'ba.ni "HL'MM, pər'vər.də"gar M'ML"H); with tied maxima (tonic = last but one of them), every Heavy syllable preceding the tonic is subtonic and the rest alternate atonic/subtonic, those adjacent to the tonic or to a Heavy syllable being atonic ('as"man.ǰah 'H"HH, "re.dɪ'o "ML'M, ka"ri.gə'ri M"ML'M).

morph.rootq: McGregor (Outline, Introduction p. xxi, following Kelkar 1968): "Inflexional endings, some other final syllables with long vowels, and prefixes sometimes do not influence stress placement; e.g. /ba'ra/ or /'bara/; ... /ni'kalna/ or /'nikalna/; /ka'ha/, but /'diya/, /'liya/ ..." with footnote: "This is especially so of prefixes. Of inflexional endings, perfective verb endings attract stress more strongly than others." The core rule itself is weight-based over the whole word…
morph.elicq: McGregor p. xxi: "Words which can show more than one stress placement when pronounced in isolation tend, on the whole, to be stressed on an earlier rather than a later syllable in connected utterances. ... In connected utterances word stress is also influenced by other factors than those discussed above, such as speech tempo, and the style and emphasis of a given utterance." Kelkar 1968 p. 26: "Hirdu has accent entirely as a part of intonation. A word may not have accent in a many-word contour-span. A word has always an accent in a single-word contour-span."…
morph.stmt: Hindi inflection and productive derivation are suffixal and post-nominal: "Nouns are inflected for number, gender and case... Verbs are inflected for person, number, gender, tense, mood, and aspect... Hindi is a verb-final language" (Koul 2008 §1.4 p.4), with case relations carried by postpositions that follow the noun ("written as separate words with nouns... but tagged to pronouns", §3.1.2 p.37) and tense/aspect auxiliaries following the verb; the only prefixes are borrowed Persian/Sanskrit derivational ones on nouns/adjectives (be-, bad-, na:-, ap-, dur-, ku-, nir-; §3.1.3.1 pp.68-69), and negation/interrogation are free preverbal / clause-initial particles.

ev.text: Hixkaryana (Derbyshire 1979) is a language of the Cariban family, and is spoken in the Amazon (northern Brazil). It has no distinctive vowel length — all surface length reflects rhythmic organization, or so-called ‘rhythmic lengthening’. ... The generalization that governs the lengthening pattern is the following: in words of three or more syllables, every even-numbered non-final open syllable is stressed, and its vowel is lengthened. This alternating length pattern can be characterized as ‘iambic’ ... final syllables in Hixkaryana never undergo vowel lengthening, and are never stressed. ... Turning now from open syllables to closed syllables, we find that these are always stressed, but tha…

652.dq: in words of three or more syllables, every even-numbered non-final open syllable is stressed, and its vowel is lengthened (Kager 1999:148); contrast Hayes 1995:206-207: 'Main stress appears to be utterly independent of metrical structure and depends instead on the intonation pattern.'

652.heavy: Closed syllables are heavy, open syllables light (Kager (17) Step 1: 'open syllables are light, closed syllables are heavy'); Kager p.155 adds 'WSP is actually undominated in Hixkaryana, for both kinds of heavy syllables, CVC and CVV, are stressed without exception', but vowel length is not distinctive (p.148 'It has no distinctive vowel length - all surface length reflects rhythmic organization'), so surface CVV arises only by iambic lengthening of stressed non-final open syllables and is derived, not an input weight class; ST1 note lists 'long vowels; closed syllables' as heavy for rhythm, following Hayes.
652.dflt: All-open-syllable words: stress and lengthening on even-numbered non-final syllables from the left (peninitial in 3-4-syllable words, 2nd and 4th in 5-syllable words); in LL disyllables the initial syllable is stressed and lengthened because finals are never stressed.
652.prule: No metrically assigned word-level main stress is described: per Hayes 1995:206-207 (carried) 'Main stress appears to be utterly independent of metrical structure and depends instead on the intonation pattern. Derbyshire (1985:182) lists five intonation contours; in four of them main stress falls on the final syllable, in the remaining one, it falls on the penult.' (StressTyp2 SPD lect codes this as fixed final primary stress.)
652.srule: Secondary (rhythmic) stresses: every closed syllable is stressed; in runs of open syllables every even-numbered non-final syllable counting from the left is stressed and its vowel lengthened, the count restarting after each closed syllable; the word-final syllable never carries rhythmic stress or length (iterative iambs L-to-R, final syllable extrametrical). Derbyshire 1999:28: 'secondary stress occurs on heavy syllables, i.e., those with final C or (prosodic) long vowels.'
652.quote: Hixkaryana (Derbyshire 1979) is a language of the Cariban family, and is spoken in the Amazon (northern Brazil). It has no distinctive vowel length — all surface length reflects rhythmic organization, or so-called ‘rhythmic lengthening’. ... The generalization that governs the lengthening pattern is the following: in words of three or more syllables, every even-numbered non-final open syllable is stressed, and its vowel is lengthened. This alternating length pattern can be characterized as ‘iambic’ ... final syllables in Hixkaryana never undergo vowel lengthening, and are never stressed. ... …
652.loc: Kager 1999 pp. 148-149 (sec. 4.3; archive.org) and p.155 (WSP undominated, with fn.5); Hayes 1995:206-207 (StressTyp2 carried entry); Hagberg thesis (fn.34)
652.idn: Hixkaryana (no dialect named; data after Derbyshire 1979); data: Kager 1999: not stated (textbook case study on Derbyshire 1979 data). Derbyshire 1965:5: 'uns 100 índios que moram ao longo do médio e alto rio Nhamundá, na divisa entre os Estados do Pará e Amazonas'; author's field trips from 1959, texts collected…
652.exq_: ﬁnal syllables in Hixkaryana never undergo vowel lengthening, and are never stressed. ... WSP is actually undominated in Hixkaryana, for both kinds of heavy syllable…

The vast majority of these are morphemically complex, consisting of a base followed by an ending [future -ni, nomic -ŋʷɨ: máqani, wárikni; causative -kna, goal -to: mɨ́nɨkna, wárikto -- initial stress; 'n…
653.tone: Stress is realized as pitch: a stressed VV́ is 'executed with a level (sometimes perceived as rising) pitch contour'; in Third Mesa some long vowels bear a falling contour ([wɨ́ɨsi] 'broom', [kóokʸaŋ] 'spider', [wɨ́ɨti] 'woman', ex. 28 p. 44), which Jeanne (sec. 1.5) derives from V + pre-consonantal laryngeal vocalized after stress assignment ('unstressed vowels are executed at a lower pitch level than stressed vowels, we hear falling tone', p. 47). Hayes 1980:126: 'stress in Hopi is manifested as high tone... The Hopi rules may thus be regarded as rules of stress placement, with the tonal realization of stress implemented by other rules.' No lexical tone system in the cited analysis; kind stays weight.

tn.quote: it was mentioned that vowel sequences in which the second member is assigned stress (i.e. [VV́]) are executed with a level (sometimes perceived as rising) pitch contour. In our Third Mesa dialect there are also long vowels which exhibit a falling pitch contour ... We assume that falling tone raises in the following fashion: laryngeal vocalization follows stress assignment, and since, in general, unstressed vowels are executed at a lower pitch level than stressed vowels, we hear falling tone. That is, the sequence [V́V] is perceived as a long vowel with falling tone.

655.dq: Hunzib word stress is not fixed, but is generally linked to the prefinal vowel of the word. (§2.5.1; §2.5.4 treats 'Word stress in nominal and verbal phrases' separately: 'In nominal phrases consisting of an initial attributive noun followed by a noun in the nominative, only the last vowel of the attributive noun is stressed')
655.dloc: §2.5 'Hunzib word stress', §2.5.1 'Position of the stress' p.28, §2.5.2 'Realisation and distinctiveness' p.29, §2.5.3.1 'Stressed affixes' p.29, §2.5.4; long vowels §2 p.22 (pages from the book's own table of contents excerpt)
655.heavy: Long vowel only. The rule is stated over vowels, not syllables: stress goes on the 'prefinal vowel', with long vowels written as VV, so a word-final long vowel (hináa, bədáa, kišáa) carries the stress = final syllable; long vowels occur only under stress and shorten when stress shifts. Closed syllables are not mentioned as heavy.
655.prule: Word stress 'is not fixed, but is generally linked to the prefinal vowel of the word' (penultimate vowel/mora): final syllable when it contains a long vowel (VV), otherwise the penultimate syllable; certain verbal affixes are 'in principle stressed'; stress is 'almost non-distinctive' (one minimal pair); irregular stresses are marked in the lexicon.
655.srule: Not mentioned in van den Berg 1995, §2.5 'Hunzib word stress' (pp.28-30, read as search excerpt; volume full-text search finds no 'secondary stress/accent', 'rhythmic' or 'alternating'): a single stressed vowel per word is described ('higher intensity of the stressed vowel compared with the other vowels of a word'); clitic groups keep the host's own stress.
655.quote: 2.5. Hunzib word stress 2.5.1. Position of the stress Hunzib word stress is not fixed, but is generally linked to the prefinal vowel of the word. It is realised as higher intensity, in some cases also as length or tone (2.5.2.). In noun and verb stems word stress usually is on the prefinal vowel, e.g. ... qoqla 'egg', ... hináa 'how?', bədáa 'like this', ... héhe 'hit', -iyáa 'cry'; kišáa 'play ... [p.22] Long vowels only occur in stressed position, where they are realised with vowel length at least by some (older) informants. Long vowels become plain when word stress shifts to another vowel.…
655.loc: §2.5 'Hunzib word stress', §2.5.1 'Position of the stress' p.28, §2.5.2 'Realisation and distinctiveness' p.29, §2.5.3.1 'Stressed affixes' p.29, §2.5.4; long vowels §2 p.22 (pages from the book's own table of contents excerpt)

655.exq_: ... Hunzib words have a different position of the word stress, e.g. akičár 'tale', andxúr 'monday', čuwadúr 'wednesday', -ežeríč' 'be glad' and a number of colour terms (see appendix 2 to the lexicon). Many loanwords are stressed on a non-prefinal vowel, e.g. surat 'picture', kağár 'paper, letter',…

morph.elicq: No statement of how stress judgments were obtained is visible in the accessible text. The description is impressionistic: 'Hunzib word stress is realised by a higher intensity of the stressed vowel compared with the other vowels of a word. Vowel length can be a concomitant feature of word stress. A relatively high tone is also a concomitant feature of word stress' (vdB 1995:29); 'Long vowels only occur in stressed position, where they are realised with vowel length at least by some (older) informants' (vdB 1995:22); data from 'fieldwork in 1990, 1992, 1993 and 1994' (preface) with texts 'recorded on tape' (p.139); irregularly stressed words 'are mentioned as such in the lexicon' (p.22).…

dqtr.text: Translation of the quoted passage: Word stress in Inga is very regular; as a general rule it falls on the penultimate syllable of each word. ('entonación' = 'intonation'.)

656.dq: El acento de la palabra en inga es muy regular; por regla general recae en la penúltima sílaba de cada palabra. (Levinsohn 1974:2; the same lesson separately treats 'entonación' of the sentence, p.1, and clitics that do or do not shift the word accent, p.7)
656.dloc: Levinsohn 1974, Lección 1, Pronunciación §2 'El acento de la palabra', p.2; Lección 2, Gramática §3 'Sufijos de énfasis (clíticos) y acento', p.7; 3sg note p.16. Maffla 1976, Corpus del inga, p.30 items 125, 127.
656.heavy: No weight criterion is stated by Levinsohn 1974 (penult 'por regla general'; final stress treated as orthographically 'regular' when the word ends in a consonant other than n, s). The weight formulation is Hayes 1995's (StressTyp2 entry note: ': closed syllables (final C is sonorant)'), i.e. a word-final syllable closed by a sonorant counts as heavy; vowel length plays no role (three short vowels a i u only).
656.prule: Levinsohn 1974: word accent very regular, as a general rule on the penultimate syllable; irregular cases marked in the orthography; 3sg-subject verb forms carry the accent on the root-final (word-final) syllable (catú '(él, ella, ello) vendió' vs catungui '(Ud.) vendió'), with the 3sg -n surfacing in some dialects. Hayes 1995 (carried, after Levinsohn 1976): final if the final syllable is heavy (closed by a sonorant), else penultimate. Maffla 1976 transcriptions show both final stress on an obstruent-closed final ([uŋgúx] 'enfermo') and penult on another ([níxpik] 'entonces').
656.srule: Optional: secondary accent may fall on alternate syllables counting leftward from the primary-accented syllable, in words (accent groups) of three or more syllables (Levinsohn 1979 §4.2, §1; transcribed e.g. à.pa.dì.ru.kár.ka.gri 'se sabe ir y llevar', p.68). No weight condition on secondaries is stated.

Se señalan y demarcan todos los indicios u ocurrencias…

Es fonémico, pero gramaticalmente predecible. Cuando la última sílaba de una palabra gramatical termina en (C 300) [= /m, n, r, y/], el acento cae sobre la última sílaba ... Cuando ciertos sufijos ocurren en posición final de palabra para componer una palabra de tres o más sílabas, el acento cae sobre la antepenúltima sílaba (/níspaka/ después, /ímata/ ¿qué?). En los demás casos el acento cae sobre la…
morph.elicq: Levinsohn 1979 (Fonología del inga) p.66-69: 'El corpus para el presente trabajo se recogió en trabajos de campo realizados en 1968 ...'; the description is framed in a prosodic hierarchy above the word: 'El grupo acentual se identifica por las siguientes características: (1) pausa final corta, (2) acento primario' (§1); 'El grupo acentual se distribuye dentro del grupo rítmico ... El grupo rítmico tiene de uno a nueve grupos acentuales' (§1.3); 'La palabra gramatical no coincide con el grupo acentual ... Opcionalmente dos palabras ocurren dentro de un solo grupo acentual /kwidawadúrmika/ es él que me cuida ... Los enclíticos ocurren opcionalmente en posición inicial dentro del grupo…
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and agglutinative: Apuntes 1978 p.5 'El inga es un idioma aglutinante; es decir, se une una multiplicidad de sufijos o desinencias a la raíz de la palabra'; Parks 1990:76 'Quechuan languages are suffixing, agglutinative and have a basic S-O-V sentence structure... There is a substantial noun suffix system, an extensive verb suffix system, and a number of independent suffixes which attach to words of any grammatical category. There is no prefixation in inherited vocabulary' (order STEM + INFLECTION + SUBORDINATOR + INDEPENDENT SUFFIX, Parks p.82-83).

[p.67] El acento secundario ocurre opcionalmente sobre el núcleo de sílabas alternas, contando desde el núcleo del grupo acentual hacia el inicio del grupo acentual.

contra.head: The published descriptions contradict each other
contra.detail: The two primaries disagree on whether Iraqw has word stress at all: Mous 1993 gives a fully predictable length+tone-conditioned word-stress rule with an initial default; Maghway 2003 (native-speaker phonologist, UDSM) states 'Phonologically, Iraqw is a non-stress language. For syllable prosodic contrast, Iraqw relies upon pitch and duration instead. Iraqw is, therefore, a tone language.'
