morph.rootq: Mous 1993:23 (as carried verbatim by StressTyp2 passage 1103; p.23 itself not in the open excerpts): 'Stress is on the penult if it has a long vowel. If the penult does not have a long vowel stress is on the final syllable if it has a high tone. If both are not the case, stress is on the first syllable.' — stated over syllable positions of the word (penult/final/first), with no reference to root or stem. The 2007 sketch has no stress statement, only 'Tone: High, Low. High tone has a limited distribution (pitch-accent)' (§1 p.5); note the High tone that licenses final stress is largely carried by suffixes/endings…
morph.elicq: No statement of the evidential basis accompanies the stress rule as carried (Mous 1993:23 via StressTyp2 1103: 'Stress is on the penult if it has a long vowel...'); Downing 2004:108 illustrates it with isolated citation nouns only ('(4) Iraqw stress (Mous 1993); accents indicate tone; the stressed vowel is underlined (a) ba/eeso 'bushbucks' (b) hlooró 'grasshopper' (c) mugúl 'collarbone' (d) wawitmo 'king' (e) bása 'south''). The sketch's only prosodic-method remark concerns intonation, not stress: 'Yes/no questions involve question intonation which is realised by a rise on the penultimate (indicated here by a circumflex on the vowel) and a slight fall on the ultimate' (§6 p.15). Maghway…
morph.stmt: Iraqw is overwhelmingly suffixing (with additional tonal, infixal and reduplicative marking): 'Possessive, demonstrative, indefinite and case markers are suffixed to the noun' (Mous 2007 §2.3), number is by 'many different suffixes to form a plural' (§2.2), verbs carry subject/number endings plus 'a durative suffix -m, a durative infix <ar>, reduplication..., middle suffix -t, causative suffix -s, inchoative suffix -w' (§8.2); the only prefixes are on the separate preverbal inflectional word 'to be' (selector) — 'four mood prefixes: the conditional bar-, the concessive tam-, the questioning m-, and the prohibitive m-' and the 3rd-person object prefix g-/ng-/k- (§7, §7.4) — plus lexical…

undet.detail: tone-with-a-stress-statement. Word prosody: a restricted two-level (H vs L) tone system with grammatical rather than lexical function, H distinctive on word-final syllables only, at most one L-to-H movement per word (patterns L* / L*H*), most words all-Low…

tones: low / accent 1 ('neutral tone', level low pitch)
high / accent 2 ('marked tone', H on the word-final syllable, 'rising')
tn.quote: There is a phonemic opposition of tone that has the properties of stress insofar as tone is assigned, mostly, to a larger domain than the mere syllable, often to the word or a whole phrase ... The available synchronic treatments of Iraqw ... have described this kind of system in terms of a two-way tonal opposition of high vs. low in which the distribution of the high tone is subject to severe restrictions ... within the boundaries of a phonological word there is only an opposition of [L0 L] vs. [L0 H]. ... In Iraqw, tone is independent of vowel length and of stress.

tn.note: Two-way H vs L, at most one word-final H ([L0 L] vs [L0 H]); Kiessling recasts it as pitch accent (accent 1 level low, accent 2 'rising'), mostly grammatical; stress separate, set by weight and H. Checked against the source (tone consistency check round 3, 2026-09-24): floating yes -> unstated (preprint p.11 sec. 3).

corr.words: As soon as the process of apocope deleted toneless final vowels in PIRQ, the resulting situation was that all nouns modified by demonstratives or possessives were left with a rising tone contour, i.e. accent 2.

657.cfw: Mous 1993, the reference grammar, states a predictable stress rule (penult if it has a long vowel, otherwise a high-toned final syllable, otherwise the first syllable) that Kiessling 2004 quotes verbatim and adopts from his own West Rift fieldwork and Downing 2004 repeats with Mous's examples, while the lone dissent, a one-line remark in Maghway 2003 that Iraqw is 'a non-stress language', comes from an article on question intonation and is most naturally read as denying contrastive stress, which Mous and Kiessling also deny.

658.heavy: a syllable (only the FIRST syllable is inspected) containing a 'strong' vowel а е и о у (a e i o u) — historically the old long vowels/diphthongs, 'even today... somewhat longer' — as opposed to a 'weak' vowel æ, ы (ə), historically short; Abaev states vowel quantity is not phonemic in modern Ossetic, so the criterion is a vowel-class (strong/peripheral vs weak/central) distinction. Codas play no role.
658.dflt: peninitial (second syllable) whenever the first vowel is weak, regardless of the second syllable's vowel
658.prule: Stress falls only on the first or second syllable of the word or accentual group: on the first syllable if it has a strong vowel (with rare exceptions), on the second syllable if the first has a weak vowel. In substantives that would be stressed on the second syllable, stress shifts to the first syllable when the noun is definite (the shift 'replaces the definite article'). Very recent Russian loans keep Russian stress.
658.srule: Not mentioned in Abaev 1964, 'Stress' §§30-32 pp. 10-11 (the section describes a single stress per word or accentual group and gives no secondary or rhythmic stresses).

RCAFL Publ. 35 (archive.org scan, in the copy consulted in). Tokens: interlinear (FLEx) Iron oral text 'Tower' (Мæсуг), speaker Islam Sasiev, Dargavs, Ossetic Grammatical Studies project (O. Belyaev, A. Vydrin, D. Erschler et al.), ossetic-studies.org/en/texts/iron, sentences 1.1-1.11.
morph.rootq: Abaev 1964 §31 p.11: 'The occurrence of stress, both in separate words and in accentual groups, is subject to the following regularities: .1 The stress falls only on the first or second syllable of the word or word-group. ... .2 If there is a strong vowel in the first syllable, then the stress falls (with rare exceptions) on the first syllable: су́дзаг 'burning', ма́͡тæрс 'do not be afraid!' .3 If there is a weak vowel in the first syllable, then the stress falls on the second syllable: сæнǽфсир 'grapes', мæ͡чи́ныг 'my book'. In substantives stressed on the second syllable, the stress is transferred to the first syllable if a definite object is involved.'…
morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was determined (native-speaker/philological description). The account explicitly covers connected speech: §30 p.10 'In the flow of speech, it is not the stress of the individual word, as in Russian, which is crucial, but rather the phrase stress. Word groups that are syntactically connected in some way, are joined together by a single stress'; §32 p.11 'The following excerpt from a folk tale, where words joined under a single stress are connected by the sign ͡, can give some notion of the rhythmical structure of Ossetic speech.' Foreword p.vi: examples were 'gleaned ... from works of Ossetic literature and folklore'.
morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing with one productive prefix class: 'Declension is agglutinative with a regular plural marker т and the same case endings for both singular and plural' (§41); 'In Ossetic, two living and highly productive methods of substantival word-formation prevail: suffixing and compounding' (§166); 'Prefixes occur in Ossetic only as preverbs' (§167), which are 'the principal means... of distinguishing the perfective aspect from the imperfective' (§105); person/tense/mood are verb suffixes, while possessors, negation and object pronouns are unstressed pro-/enclitics joined to a neighbouring word under one phrase stress (§30, §70, §155, §216).

658.sec_quote: § 30. In Ossetic, the stress is expiratory (intensive). In the flow of speech, it is not the stress of the individual word, as in Russian, which is crucial, but rather the phrase stress. Word groups that are syntactically connected in some way, are joined together by a single stress. Thus, a substantial number of words appear without independent stress.

tn.quote: § 9. ФОНЕТИЧЕСКОЕ УДАРЕНИЕ Ударением называется выделение одного слога в слове или группе слов при помощи усиления голоса или повышения тона. Если ударение выражается в усилении голоса, то его принято называть силовым, динамическим, или экспираторным. Такое ударение действует во многих языках, в том числе и в осетинском. … на почве иранских языков постепенно выявилась тенденция, в силу которой тоническое ударение уступило место силовому … Эта тенденция ярко проявилась в осетинском языке.
tn.translation: §9. Phonetic stress. Stress is the singling out of one syllable in a word or group of words by increased force of voice or by raising of pitch. If stress is expressed by increased force of voice it is called force, dynamic or expiratory stress. Such stress operates in many languages, Ossetian among them. … on Iranian soil a tendency gradually emerged by which tonic (pitch) accent gave way to force accent … This tendency showed itself vividly in Ossetian.
tn.cite: Ахвледиани, Г. С. (ред.). 1963. Грамматика осетинского языка. Том I: Фонетика и морфология. Орджоникидзе: Северо-Осетинский научно-исследовательский институт [Северо-Осетинское книжное изд-во]. («Введение» / исторический комментарий -- В. И. Абаев; «Фонетика», incl. 'Ударение и ритмика' §§9-11 -- М. И. Исаев.)
tn.locator: p. 49, 'Ударение и ритмика', §9 'Фонетическое ударение' + p. 31, Введение: Исторический комментарий, point 3
tn.note: No tone: Ossetian stress is of the dynamic (force) type, not the tonic (pitch) type; historically the Indo-European pitch accent gave way to force stress. No tone inventory is described.

658.cfw: Abaev 1964, the reference grammars of Akhvlediani 1963 and Bagaev 1965, Dzakhova's 2010 instrumental study of eight speakers and Thordarson 2009 all give the same rule: stress falls on the first or second syllable, the first when it holds a strong (long) vowel and the second when it holds a weak (short) one, with a shift to the first syllable marking definiteness, and they differ only on how often strong-strong words take initial stress and on a few lexical exceptions.

659.dq: In Italian, main stress can be found on any of the last three syllables of a word. There is general consent that this is due to lexical stress.
659.dloc: Krämer 2009 author-copy (15 pp.) pp. 1-3 (abstract, sec. 1, exx. 1-5; fn. 3 p. 4 for H=CVC) and p. 14 (sec. 5 Conclusion); supporting generalisations sec. 3 pp. 5-6, 9-10; Rogers & d'Arcangeli 2004 JIPA 34(1) p. 119 ('Stress is phonemic.')
659.heavy: Heavy = syllable closed by a consonant (H = CVC, L = CV; codas incl. first half of geminates); vowel length is not contrastive ('long vowels occur in stressed open syllables only'), so CVV plays no role in weight.
659.dflt: Disputed/indeterminate: penult (D'Imperio & Rosenthall 1999; lexical majority) or antepenult (Morén 2001); Krämer's nonce test: LLL words split ~50/50, LLLL strongly penult; never final.
659.prule: Lexical (contrastive) main stress on one of the last three syllables of the word (nouns; up to fourth-last in verbs, further with enclitics), shown by minimal pairs (mɛ́ːta/metá, áŋkora/aŋkóːra). Lexical frequency ~80% penult, ~18% antepenult, ~2% final. Weight sub-generalization: a closed (CVC) penult attracts stress, i.e. antepenultimate stress is (near-)excluded when the penult is heavy, with 'only a small set' of exceptions, mostly place names/loans (pólizza, mándorla type). Default in all-light words is indeterminate (penult or antepenult; speakers split); heavy antepenult does not attract stress; final stress never default.
659.srule: Optional and non-distinctive. Krämer 2009: 'In words of sufficient length secondary stress is optional' (no placement rule; his four-syllable candidate (ròka)(páː)do and fn. 7 put it word-initially). Placement per Bertinetto & Loporcaro 2005: in non-compound polysyllables secondary ('rhythmical') prominences are movable and variable in number, located by tempo and phrase rhythm with at least one unstressed syllable between stresses and a tendency not to shift the rhythmical stress to the immediate right of the syllable stressed on the preceding cycle (pràticaménte rather than pratìcaménte; lubrìficatóio ~ lùbrificatóio ~ emphatic lùbrifìcatóio all possible); lexically fixed only in compounds, on the syllable that bears primary stress in the isolated word (àpriscátole). (Vogel & Scalise 1982 / Peperkamp 1997, words in isolation: initial secondary unless it would clash with the main stress, no clashes, no run of three unstressed syllables.)

tn.quote: Si incontra spesso il termine tono anche negli studi relativi a lingue, come l’italiano, nelle quali la variazione di altezza tonale ha valore solo a livello postlessicale, cioè in relazione alla frase (§ 3.4). In questo caso, il termine può indicare uno degli elementi primitivi che compongono i ‘morfemi’ o ‘fonemi’ tonali oppure un elemento di una sequenza distintiva (per es., in italiano, un tono basso caratterizza l’accento tonale principale delle frasi dichiarative neutre, descritto come discendente; si pensi alla pronuncia di mela in Maria mangia una mela).
tn.translation: The term tone is also often met in studies of languages, such as Italian, in which variation in pitch height has value only at the post-lexical level, i.e. in relation to the sentence (sec. 3.4). In this case the term may denote one of the primitive elements that make up the tonal 'morphemes' or 'phonemes', or an element of a distinctive sequence (e.g., in Italian, a low tone characterises the main pitch accent of neutral declarative sentences, described as falling; think of the pronunciation of mela in Maria mangia una mela).
tn.cite: Gili Fivela, Barbara (2011). prosodia. In Raffaele Simone (ed.), Enciclopedia dell'Italiano, vol. II. Roma: Istituto della Enciclopedia Italiana Treccani. Online edition, treccani.it.
tn.note: No lexical tone: pitch is distinctive only post-lexically (intonation), unlike Mandarin or Swedish. Word stress free and distinctive; its main correlate in Italian is duration ('dynamic' accent).
